newsitem.title: USA: Start of new Congress marked by optimism on budget.
newsitem.headline: Start of new Congress marked by optimism on budget.

text.p: Congress will reconvene on Tuesday with a new sense of optimism that last year's budget brawls can be replaced by a deal to wipe out the deficit by 2002.
"We've got a better shot at a deficit-elimination deal than we've had in decades," said Stan Collender, managing director at Burson-Marsteller.

The lessons learned during the last Congress, when Republicans took control of both houses for the first time in 40 years and had to deal with a president from the other party, were expected to lead to smoother sailing on the budget this year.

Two government shutdowns during the budget tussles of the last session backfired on Republicans, who were blamed by the public for the impasse. So the new Congress was more likely to aim for compromise than confrontation, analysts said.

"There is first of all a sense that we ought to be able to put together a budget package plan that gets to balance in the year 2002," a senior budget committee aide said. "I think there is a sense that we can do this both at the White House and Congress."
A key factor behind the optimism was an expectation that government deficit projections for 2002 will be smaller than previous estimates, making the zero deficit target easier to reach.

White House deficit projections were expected to be closer to Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates, removing one area of discord. During the last session the wide gap between the two figures created contention between Republicans and the administration over what was needed to balance the budget.
Administration estimates for the deficit in 2002 will be closer to $150 billion, while CBO estimates will be near $200 billion, Collender said.

The lead on budget talks was expected to shift to the Senate from the House. Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, was seen as more willing to work out a deal than House Speaker Newt Gingrich was.
Gingrich's influence was likely to wane, at least initially, as he struggled to repair damage to his reputation from ethics violations.

Clinton, beginning his final term as president, and Representative John Kasich of Ohio, in his last term as chairman of the House Budget Committee, may have more incentive to reach a budget agreement before they leave their positions, a congressional aide said.
The CBO was scheduled to report its "baseline" budget projections Jan. 28 when the agency's director testifies before the Senate Budget Committee.
The baseline projects the cost of federal programmes in the absence of policy changes, and is used by Congress as the basis for estimating the cost of new proposals.

Senate Republicans plan to hold a retreat Jan. 9 and 10 in Washington to set an agenda, including their direction on budget issues. Clinton was expected to release his budget in the first week of February.
Congress will vote again on a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution this year, with the Senate expected to start debate on it in early February.

Passage would require a two-thirds majority yes vote by each chamber. Analysts said it appeared the Senate had the votes to approve, but the outcome was less certain in the House. If passed, the states would have to ratify the amendment -- a process that could take years.

On the tax front, House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, identified two priorities -- a child tax credit and broad-based capital gains tax cuts, a committee spokesman said.
Archer had a one-on-one meeting with Clinton in December to set the groundwork for the tax issues and came out "very hopeful" an agreement could be reached, the spokesman said.
